S

Situation

Six tools to create one order.

Situation 1 of 3

The order journey

Every order starts with a handoff, so the story starts there.

S1.1Where the Order Processor sits

A salesperson gets the requirement from the client by call or PO, creates a Quote to match the PO, and assigns a POM ID to that Quote. The system or an admin then assigns the POM ID to an Order Processor in the Back Office. The Order Processor works on it in the PO Assistant to create the order, and the Order Team checks the order details.

If the data conflicts anywhere, the Order Processor suspends the POM ID and it goes back to Sales for resolution.

S1.2The tool they use: ABBYY

To read the PO, Order Processors used ABBYY, a third-party tool. ABBYY does one job. It fetches the information from the PO copy and lists it in a single-column form of parameters.

Key takeaway

ABBYY could read the PO. It couldn't tell users whether the PO was right.

Situation 2 of 3

The problem

Once you see what ABBYY does, the gap is easy to spot.

A correct order depends on checking the PO data against Dell's own information: the Quote, OEI, and the Hold tools. None of those exist inside ABBYY.

Users had no way to verify, in the tool that held the data, whether the data was correct.

S2.1Where the missing information lives

Key takeaway

The information users had to check lived in other systems, and ABBYY had no way to reach it.

Situation 3 of 4

The real problem

That gap didn't stay empty. Users filled it themselves.

The work didn't happen in ABBYY. It happened around it.

To add, verify, and correct data, users left ABBYY and went into the Dell ecosystem: Quote, OEI, and Hold. Then they went into tools they had set up themselves: Excel and Notepad. One order meant six tools and a lot of switching.

Key takeaway

Design for Shree's whole job: Compare PO and Quote information and Update the information if any mismatch is there.

Situation 4 of 4

The current journey

Mapping the actual workflow revealed how convoluted the process had become.

T

Task

Cut order-creation time by 30% in three months, for Shree.

Task 1 of 2

Dell's goal

The situation made the case for change, and Dell set a target.

Dell decided to build a new tool in-house to speed up order creation. The first target was a 30% reduction in the time it takes. I had three months to reach a final design draft.

Task 2 of 2

Who I designed for

Before designing anything, we needed to know who we were designing for.

We designed for Shree, a Senior Assistant on the Order Management team. She is the person in the middle of the seven stops on the map above.

Shree

Senior Assistant
Location
Hyderabad, India
Team
Order Management
Daily target
50 orders

Highly experienced at getting the job done, even when the system gets in the way. She built her own support layer of spreadsheets, manual comparisons, and recovery strategies to connect the work.

Personality
IntrovertExtrovert
AnalyticalCreative
BusyTime rich
MessyOrganized
IndependentTeam player

“I know how to get the order through. The problem is how many places I have to go to get there.”

Goals
  • Hit the target of 50 successfully processed orders a day.
  • Capture all mandatory details in the PO Assistant.
  • Pass incomplete orders back to sales reps without delay.
  • Get through the ABBYY flow without detours to other tools.
Mapping My Observation
  • ABBYY shows the PO data but not the Quote, OEI, or hold information she has to check.
  • POs that arrive without mandatory details force rework and bounces to sales reps.
  • The 50-a-day target has to be balanced against the need to be careful and concise.
Needs and expectations
  • Clear validation: an immediate flag when a PO is missing mandatory details.
  • Smooth routing: one click to pass an incomplete PO back to the responsible sales rep.
  • Trustworthy AI: reliable extraction from ABBYY and reliable judgement from DSA, so she doesn't have to double-check the automation.
  • Focus: a concise interface that supports careful work without clutter.
Receive
Review
Verify
Correct
Create
Recover

Her primary job: turn a PO and a Quote into a valid order, and recover when something fails.

Key takeaway

Design for Shree's whole job: get a PO and a Quote to a valid order, and recover when something fails.

A

Action

Nine steps, from using the tool myself to a tested design.

Action 1 of 9

Become a user

Before asking anyone anything, I wanted to feel the work myself.

A1.1Walking the workflow

I used ABBYY the way an Order Processor does, working through an order before I spoke to a single user. That gave me my own view of where the tool stops and the manual work starts.

Key takeaway

Every field got a decision: editable, read-only, or defaulted from the Quote.

Action 2 of 9

Mapping My Observation

Using ABBYY showed me where it hurt. I mapped that pain before testing it on others.

A2.1The hypothesis

I started with one hypothesis: the process is complicated because users have to switch between applications to complete their tasks. I built the research to test that, not to collect feature requests.

A2.2Mapping the pain points

The map follows one common scenario: the information on the PO and the Quote differs, so the user has to put the order on hold. It touches ABBYY, DSA, SharePoint, OEI Governance, and Notepad, which users open to avoid formatting issues.

Each stop added manual work. Users downloaded the PO documents to their desktop to check them by hand, checked DSA to see if the order already existed, looked up OEI instructions for the customer, then typed the hold details into SharePoint and checked DSA again to confirm the hold.

The map also marked what users wished for: verify the order and Quote automatically, find OEI instructions when needed, and fill the Sales Hold Tracker for them. Those became design requirements.

Key takeaway
  • No Proper / Wrong extraction of data from PO copy in ABBYY.
  • Switching between tools while keeping the quotes data in notepad or paper.
  • Source of truth PO is missing on Quotes Page.
  • Validity of Quote is missing on ABBYY, I have to use DSA for that.
  • Action like change address or information is missing.
Action 3 of 9

User Research

Now, I need to hear from Experts what they feel about the process and what is missing.

A3.1The interviews

I ran 20 remote behavioral interviews across global sales roles, 30 to 45 minutes each. I built the sessions around the real work rather than around feature requests.

Working environment

Monitor count, screen resolution, scaling, and physical setup.

Order creation

Mandatory information, verification, ownership boundaries, and completion criteria.

ABBYY walk-through

Extraction, Quote versions, addresses, holds, errors, and recovery.

Starting from the real work helped separate what users say they want from what they actually do.

A3.2In their words

“ABBYY pulls the incorrect PO Copy at times.”

“Errors on quote/account are not displayed.”

“When we put the POM ID on Sales Hold with explanation, why do we still have to fill all the information in SharePoint.”

A3.3The survey

To put numbers on what I heard, I followed the interviews with a survey of 82 participants covering tools, quotes, errors, satisfaction, and work setup.

Key takeaway

Twenty interviews and 82 survey responses were built to test one idea: users switch applications because the system does not connect the work.

Action 4 of 9

Findings

The interviews and survey gave me data. Findings is what that data said.

A4.1What the interviews showed

Order Processors weren't struggling with one difficult interface. They were making up for gaps in the system.

Verification happened outside the product

Users manually compared PO documents, Quotes, and extracted data.

Important information lived elsewhere

OEI, SharePoint, email, Excel, and local files filled the gaps.

Small data issues created large effort

Names, alphanumeric values, addresses, GOALs, payment methods, and Quote versions all created edge-case work.

A4.2What the survey showed

Three questions mattered most.

Two numbers stood out. Half of all new Quote versions exist to update Bill-To information, and another 34% to update Ship-To. Users were creating whole new versions to fix address details.

A4.3Satisfaction scores

Users rated the tools well. Creating one order still took 12 minutes on average.

8.03/10
ABBYY

Satisfaction with order creation.

8.54/10
DSA

Satisfaction with order creation.

12 min
Average time

To create one order.

66%
Hangs and crashes

Reported in the legacy tool.

Other findings pointed the same way: 16% reported consistently incorrect extraction, 58% relied on external Excel spreadsheets, and 68% reported at least one preventable data-entry error a week.

Users had adapted to the tools they knew, even though the workflow between those tools was costing them time and trust.

That changed the strategy. We didn't need to replace everything users knew. We needed to keep what worked and remove the movement between systems.

A4.4The work environment

Data from 82 participants challenged the picture of a modern, multi-screen setup.

96%
Single monitor

One workspace, not a command center.

64%
150% scaling

Content had to work with enlarged system UI.

38%
1280×720

The viewport could be highly constrained.

1
Source of truth

The PO had to stay visible while working.

The other large group, 32%, used a 1920×1080 screen. The layout had to hold up at both ends.

Key takeaway

Users rated their tools well, but the workflow between them took 12 minutes, on a single small screen.

Action 5 of 9

Synthesis

The findings were a long list. Synthesis turned them into a diagnosis and a direction.

A5.1Affinity map

I clustered what users liked, disliked, and expected from ABBYY and DSA into one affinity map.

A5.2The diagnosis

1

Fragmentation

Users switched between ABBYY, DSA, OEI, SharePoint, Notepad, Excel, and other tools.

2

Cognitive load

Dense interfaces buried warnings, and users had to remember where information lived.

3

Data uncertainty

Automatic extraction saved some work but introduced enough errors that users verified everything by hand.

4

Eroded trust

Repeated errors and failures led users to build their own checks, spreadsheets, and recovery strategies.

5

Compliance and consistency gaps

The experience had significant accessibility issues and departed from enterprise design standards.

A5.3What to keep

I didn't assume everything about ABBYY had to go. Users liked several things, and we kept them.

One-screen processing

Multiple Quotes and shipping groups handled in one place.

Default-to-Quote

Much of the Quote information came into the workflow automatically.

PO visibility

The source PO stayed available while processing.

Mandatory-field guidance

Important information was surfaced during order creation.

Easy editing

Shipping and extracted information could be adjusted directly.

Integrated actions

Some hold and notification workflows were already built in.

A5.4Design decisions

Each finding turned into a design decision:

Remove local downloads

Keep the source PO inside the workflow.

Remove external tracking

Bring comments and hold management into the tool.

Reduce duplicate entry

Surface and reuse existing information.

Make errors actionable

Take the user to where the issue can be fixed.

Bring validation closer

Show required information where the Order Processor decides.

Key takeaway

Consolidate the workflow without forcing users to relearn it.

Action 6 of 9

MoSCoW

The direction gave us more ideas than three months could hold, so we had to choose.

A6.1Aligning the team

I took the findings to Product Management, Design, and Development, including the architect, before drawing any screens. Once we had approval, we moved into screen design.

Research findings
Review with PM, Design, Architect
Approval
Screen design

A6.2Prioritizing the scope

The research produced a long list of possible improvements and we had three months. I ran a MoSCoW workshop with Product Management and Engineering to decide what went in. The field audit fed the first Must-have.

The board sorted the ideas into four groups. Nothing was ruled out: Won't have stayed empty.

Must have
  • All necessary sections and parameters in the new design
  • Extraction error and resolution management
  • Three-way comparison of Quote, PO, and PO document
  • Hold management
  • Editing of PO data and Quote data
  • Comment section
  • Payment method
  • SKU data
Should have
  • OEI and other validation
  • Quote overrides on the page
  • Document upload or replace
  • Working on multiple POs
  • Confirmation for cancel or complete order
  • CFO section on the page
Could have
  • Resizable PO copy section
  • PO deadline status

To protect the release, we cut two Should-haves: document uploads and on-page Quote overrides.

Key takeaway

Solve the moments that create the most friction before adding breadth.

Action 7 of 9

Crazy 8 with the product team

With the scope agreed, it was time to generate ideas together.

A7.1The exercise

I ran a Crazy 8 exercise with the product team. Crazy 8 is a timed sketching exercise: everyone sketches eight quick ideas for the same problem in eight minutes, so the room moves past the first obvious answer.

A7.2Fields Mapping as per DSA UX Patterns

Following the Crazy 8 ideation, we mapped all extracted and mandatory order-processing fields against standard Dell DSA (Digital Sales Assistant) UX patterns. This ensured consistent layout hierarchy, input controls, error states, and inline validation across both Quote and PO data structures.

I inventoried every field in ABBYY. The audit covered Comments, PO Bill To, PO Number, Payment Method, MABD, Tax, Quote, Shipping Group, and Line Item.

For each field I recorded whether users could edit it or only read it, and whether it defaulted from the Quote. A second list captured the fields users check in the Quote that ABBYY never showed, such as PO Type, PO Payment Method, Quote Bill To Customer Number, Quote Shipping Charges, and Quote Taxes.

Key takeaway
  1. PO Copy should be visible on Right hand side.
  2. They want to compare PO Data and Quote Data side by side.
Action 8 of 9

Draw some options

I took the strongest ideas and drew them out.

A8.1What should stay visible?

A8.2Three layouts

With the PO fixed on the right, the open question was how to lay out the active order on the left, where users compare the PO with the Quote. We explored three answers.

A8.3The annotated direction

I annotated the design to explain what each area was for.

  • Open the OEI instructions in a new tab with the search criteria already filled in.
  • Email, comments, and the option to create a new Quote version sit together at the top.
  • Open the Quote in a new tab if it is required.
  • PO information and Quote information sit side by side.
Key takeaway

The PO stays visible on the right. Three layouts competed for how to work the order on the left.

Action 9 of 9

Final options

Several options, one product. This is how we chose.

A9.1The final screen

The final workspace is built around one source of truth: the original PO stays on the right while the order is worked on the left.

Source of truth

The PO stays visible in a PDF viewer with a file selector and zoom, so users never download it to check it.

Errors that lead somewhere

Errors, warnings, and info sit at the top. The error message links to the section where it can be fixed.

Five tabs, one order

POM Information, Overview, Additional Information, Shipping Groups, and CFO Notifications keep the long form in order.

Compare and correct

Quote and Purchase Order values sit in two columns for the overview, Bill To, Ship To, and line items, with Edit and Override Validation in place.

Comments and holds

PO documents, comments, and Hold Management live in POM Information, with Cancel and Suspend POM Record one click away.

Actions up top

Create Order, Create Quote Version, OEI Instructions, and the Large Value and Tax Exempt holds are always in reach.

Key takeaway

Six tools became one workspace. Users see the source, verify the information, resolve the issue, and create the order in the same place.

Result 3 of 3

What I learned

Looking back over the whole path.

The biggest lesson was that high familiarity does not necessarily mean a workflow is good.

Users had learned to work around ABBYY and the surrounding systems. They maintained spreadsheets, double-checked extracted information, switched applications, and developed their own recovery strategies. Instead of reading those behaviors as resistance to change, I treated them as evidence.

Key takeaway

The real design work was finding which parts of the workflow to keep, and which sources of friction the system should finally take away.
